title: Bullish Industry Pros Are Turning Wine’s Slump into a Shopping Spree
summary:
With a historic surplus of vineyards and wineries for sale, industry pros with cash flow are snapping up dream vineyards and estates.

The post Bullish Industry Pros Are Turning Wine’s Slump into a Shopping Spree appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
We’ve all seen the headlines: consumption is slumping, buyers are scarce, and the wine market is no longer flush with cash.

This has caused many winery owners and conglomerate strategists to batten down the hatches by lowering overhead, cutting marketing and travel budgets, and streamlining SKUs. 

Jean-Charles Boisset, meanwhile, just bought a 350-acre estate in the heart of California wine country.

Late September, the Burgundy-born, Napa-based winemaker announced that he had purchased Artesa Estate in Carneros from Spanish giant Raventós Codorníu.

Expanding in a global downturn is not the most conventional approach, nor is it one most accountants would approve of. But for some seemingly-omniscient winery owners, this inflection point is an opportunity.

Buying the Farm

The appeal of Artesa is obvious. The Carneros estate oversees 350 acres of land (150 planted to vines) from Napa’s southern reaches to the tippy-top of Mt. Veeder. Included in the sale is its existing inventory and its behemoth structures, such as the pyramid-shaped tasting room and serene reflecting pools. 

“It’s gorgeous—artistic, powerful, energetic, vibrant,” says Boisset, who already has a wide Napa portfolio that includes Oakville Grocery, the Calistoga Depot, Raymond Vineyards, Elizabeth Spencer, and JCB St. Helena.

The estate is located in the south of Napa, where cool breezes from the San Pablo Bay coax out acidity from the grapes, allowing producers to make premium sparkling wines.

When the opportunity to purchase Artesa found him through friends, Boisset jumped on it. At the guidance of strategic advisors, Raventós is pivoting to focus on Spanish and Argentinian projects.

“I’ve always wanted this site,” says Boisset. “I’ve been after it for twenty years, and I’ve missed the opportunity three times.”

With a historic surplus of vineyards and wineries for sale, similarly savvy companies with cash flow are snapping up dream vineyards and estates as they are listed. If you have capital and creativity, why not take advantage of the opportunity?

This year alone, Italy’s Santa Margherita purchased Domaine Lumineux in the Dundee Hills with the intention of making sparkling wine, Crimson Wine Group picked up Raeburn in Sonoma to fill a Chardonnay gap in their portfolio, and Trinchero acquired Mumm Napa from Pernod Ricard, hoping to get a stronger hold onto the sparkling category.

“Periods of disruption create opportunities for companies willing to invest rather than retreat,” says John Sutton, CEO of The Wine Group, parent company to Beringer, Benziger, and a dozen-plus other brands.

Filling in Blank Pages

Jackson Family Wines, a California-based wine giant, has used this inflection point to invest in new markets and fill in white spaces.

Noticing that consumers were drifting towards white blends, they snapped up Big Salt—John House and Ksenija Kostic House’s white blend-centered Oregon brand—in mid-March. 

Eying the potential of Britain’s Champagne-y limestone soils and the high quality of the bubbles, Jackson Family hired former Gusbourne winemaker Charlie Holland, purchased 60 acres in the Crouch Valley, and, in 2023, announced a move to make sparkling and still English wines. Last year, they released their first bottling: a still Chardonnay.

2023 also marked JFW’s purchase of Blue Grouse and Quill, a Cowichan Valley winery on British Columbia’s Vancouver Island.

The company’s strategy: to continue making the wines of Freemark Abbey, Cardinale, La Crema, Kendall-Jackson, and Siduri, while simultaneously beginning to chase cooler-climate sites and wineries that show longer-term viticultural potential, especially amid an ever-changing climate. 

These moves are signs of expansion and investment, yes, but they’re also a way of future-proofing in a fluctuating, disaster-prone climate. If California’s viticultural potential ever softens, they have a back-up plan—a way to continue making Chardonnay and Pinot Noir with grace.

Riding Out the Downturn

Big mergers and acquisitions are just the news that makes headlines. Other major players are investing time and resources into vineyard management or innovation in an effort to fortify their wines in the future.

Joseph Phelps Vineyards, a Napa Valley stalwart, has used the quiet time to rip out vines that weren’t performing well or planted in the wrong direction and replace them with better clones or varieties. 

The Wine Group is funneling time and investments into new beverage formats and innovations. “The future of wine will not exactly look like its past,” says Sutton. “We believe wine has a vibrant future—but the companies that thrive will be the ones that evolve with the consumer.”

Last year, the Group scooped up St. Agrestis’ Phony Negroni, a line of single-serve, zero-proof Negroni riffs. 

In 2025, they purchased a swath of labels from Constellation Brands, including Meiomi, Robert Mondavi Private Selection, and Woodbridge. More importantly, the agreement included three facilities and 2,670 hectares (owned and leased) of vines. This, Sutton says, has helped ramp up their in-house innovation.

They’re no longer just a wine group, so to speak—they’re digging into non-alc and RTDs.  “M&A is only one part of our strategy,” Sutton says. “We’re also innovating across formats, packaging, flavors, sizes, price points, and alcohol levels to reflect how consumers’ preferences and occasions are changing.”

“Our goal is to create more ways for consumers to engage with our brands—and more on-ramps into the wine category,” he adds. “We’re optimistic because moments of change reward companies that listen to consumers, invest with conviction, and keep evolving.”

The Road Ahead

It’s worth noting that not everyone can be bullish in such a market. 

A lot of these endeavors boil down to money. Big wineries and wine groups have more of it, which makes it easier to invest resources and funds into future-proofing and expanding. These grand ideas of growth and innovation are hard to grasp for wineries who are just trying to stay out of the red and survive. 

Many of the properties and vineyards up for sale are independent and family-run, selling because it’s no longer economically possible to continue in the current climate.

Cain Vineyard & Winery, after struggling to rebound from the 2020 Glass Fire, found it best to sell their Spring Mountain estate to someone better equipped financially and emotionally to navigate the current downturn. Other wineries are selling off land because the cost of farming is too high to sustain the vines, tasting room sales have struggled, and the supply chain is backlogged. It’s not an easy time to make and sell wine. 

Boisset is an optimist. “Yes, the market is a challenge right now. But wine is going to be here for thousands of more years,” says Boisset. “It’s always a good time to invest in wine.”

title: A Glowing Tunnel of Sake Bottles Leads to This Bucket List Maldives Restaurant
summary:
Designed by Tokyo architect Noriyoshi Muramatsu, Saoke has one of the most extensive collection of sakes in the Maldives.

The post A Glowing Tunnel of Sake Bottles Leads to This Bucket List Maldives Restaurant appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
One of the world’s most spectacular—and unusual—displays of sake and wine is floating above water in the middle of the Indian Ocean. 

Illuminated, bookcase-like shelves of rare, niche, and hard-to-find bottles line both sides of the long wooden pier that leads to Saoke, an overwater Japanese-inspired restaurant. Located at Joali Maldives, a glamorous, art-covered resort on the archipelago’s tiny Muravandhoo Island, the restaurant was designed by the celebrated Tokyo architect Noriyoshi Muramatsu.

In recent years, the highest-end cellars and wine storage systems at restaurants, hotels, and private residences have become increasingly architectural and design-oriented—hence the trend of the at-home wine room, which treats storage like sculpture. But we have yet to see an aisle of bottles quite like this, let alone one suspended above a remote stretch of clear emerald ocean. As if the Maldives weren’t idyllic enough, this immersive installation ups the antes for drinks-loving travelers.

To reach Saoke, guests must walk through this bottle-lined entryway as waves lap beneath them. With over 40 labels, the restaurant has one of the most extensive sake collections in the Maldives, in addition to its 250-plus wine labels. With the structure’s calming wood elements and its soft organic glow, one has the feeling of floating in a paper lantern. 

But the cellar display itself, more than simply a container for standout bottles, is art that gets people talking. It’s a visual drinks menu you can peruse before stepping foot in the restaurant.

“Guests often stop to admire the bottles, ask questions, or recognise labels they have enjoyed before,” says James Badjie, head sommelier at Joali Maldives. “Many use the collection as a starting point when deciding what to drink, which opens the door to conversations with our team about different styles, producers, and pairings.”

The Design

The original design brief given to Muramatsu described the inspiration for Saoke as “a flower that lives in an overwater zen garden,” says Duygu Tatar, the resort’s senior director of marketing and communications. And so the serene feeling begins on that long entryway aisle that evokes a Japanese garden pathway, illuminated by the vertical shelves of sake on one side (entering the restaurant) and wine on the other (exiting the restaurant).

Muramatsu, who has designed many interiors for the global restaurant chain Zuma, is known for his use of natural materials, and here, timber, stone, and gentle backlighting keep the spotlight on the bottles themselves.

“We wanted to combine the Maldivian and Japanese feeling over water,” says Tatar. “[Muramatsu] is a super guy who understood very well.” At the end of the bottle-lined path, guests arrive at a minimalist stone bar, which marks the beginning of the restaurant and frames a spectacular view of the ocean.

The Collection

The sakes at Saoke run the gamut from high-end benchmark labels to rare niche selections from family-run producers. Badjie’s current favorite bottle is Dassai 23 Junmai Daiginjo, which he pairs with the restaurant’s miso-marinated, bamboo-wrapped black cod, cooked over charcoal in a robata grill. Other unique bottles on offer include Ginrei Gassan Junmai Ginjo (aged in natural snow stores), the high-acid Cowboy Yamahai (meant to be paired with rich meat dishes), and Sa Kén Ice (a Champagne-method sparkling sake produced in Italy.)

Saoke’s collection also goes beyond standard Japanese plum wine offerings with luxury umeshu selections and rare aged plum liqueurs. And of course, the restaurant’s wine list is equally thoughtful. One of Badjie’s current favorite wines in the collection is CR1 Redstone from Capelands Wine Estate in Somerset West, South Africa. 

“The biggest challenge is logistics, bringing exceptional wines and sakes to a remote island while ensuring they arrive in perfect condition,” says Badjie. “Once they are here, maintaining consistent temperature, humidity, and storage conditions is essential.” For that reason, most of the wine collection is stored in the resort’s large climate-controlled cellar on shore, where guests can book private tastings with Badjie and taste a globe-trotting selection of rare vintages. Sakes are stored in Saoke’s chiller.

Why It Stands Out

Integrated into the architecture itself, the Saoke cellar display is the entrance, immersing guests in the glowing collection for several moments before they arrive at the bar. It is intentionally designed as a conversation piece to kick off exchanges guests will inevitably have with the somm—about brewing styles, regions, and pairing recommendations. 

While Japanese concepts have become more popular in the Maldives, it is rare to find such an extensive and prominently displayed sake collection anywhere in the world, let alone in the middle of the Indian Ocean. “We have a very detailed program for wine, but sake is also something that—you cannot find this level of service in the Maldives,” says Tatar. “It’s kind of like a sake workshop for guests.”

title: NoLow Isn’t a Passing Fad—and It Deserves Your Respect
summary:
The NoLow category is skyrocketing as more wine lovers gravitate toward the "less but better" model. So, we’re launching a NoLow blind tasting program.

The post NoLow Isn’t a Passing Fad—and It Deserves Your Respect appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
In the United States alone, non-alcoholic beverage retail sales crossed $1 billion by the end of 2025. 

Worldwide, the total volume of NA beer, wine, RTDs, and spirits grew 9% last year. And from 2024 to 2029, that number is expected to grow 36%—to hit 18 billion servings. According to IWSR, that’s enough for every person on the planet to consume two each. 

There is also significant growth in low-alcohol products, too. In 2025, the low-alcohol market was valued at 8 million and is expected to reach 8.3 million by the end of this year.

Obviously, with numbers like that, it’s not just teetotalers partaking in this NA surge. Nielsen reports that 92% of consumers who buy non-alcoholic products also buy alcohol.

It’s no surprise if you follow the pattern. In the years following Covid’s over-consumption, why wouldn’t we have a corrective cycle? 

However, the idea that it’s merely a reaction is what needs to be fully debunked. Wellness culture is here to stay, but more importantly, so are GLP-1s. And you know what? The “less but better” model is one that perfectly aligns with the philosophy of a true wine lover.

This is why Wine Enthusiast is launching a new NoLow blind-tasting program. The category that may have appeared to be a passing fad at first is now a mainstay—and deserves your respect.

Quantity and Quality

The technology that supports this category has come a long way in the last ten years. I sat down with Giesen, one of the original high-quality NoLow producers, about a year ago at ProWein. We tasted what was, at the time, their unreleased highest-quality 0% New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc. I was stunned. The technology they had championed for years had evolved, and so had the quality of the flavor, aromas, and, ultimately, the enjoyment.

Last week, I met with Dante Catena, who helped launch an extremely innovative lineup of NoLow wines and botanicals, Domaine EdeM. The effort that went into making these would shock those who assume there’s anything being “removed” or simplified to create these types of beverages. They were thoughtfully produced, and the botanical lineup especially brought a complexity that reminded me of sipping a compelling Italian amaro.

We can no longer go on ignoring this increasingly high-quality category. It is a force, and it is officially a part of what American drinkers need guidance on. We are here to help.

A New Rating System

Wine Enthusiast’s reviews of NoLow wines, spirits, and RTDs will be handled differently from our usual 100-point scores. Because the process and structure of these products are incomparable to those that are traditionally vinified, we are using a five-star rating system. 

Reviews will evaluate factors such as balance, flavor, aroma, texture, and the overall drinking experience of the products submitted within the context of their respective categories. That will give them space to not be held to an illogical standard, but rather to be judged against their true peers. The star system further reinforces this differentiation while giving consumers a universally recognized guide for purchasing.

Wine Enthusiast Spirits Reviewer Kara Newman is handling NoLow spirits, while Writer-At-Large Cheron Cowan is covering NoLow RTDs and other products marketed at no- or low-alcohol, such as tea-based beverages and infused or macerated products. 

Conscious consumption advocate Abe Zarate, known as SoberSomm on Instagram, is joining the team to review NoLow wines.

Get to know our fabulous crew of NoLow reviewers—plus, their favorite drinks at the moment.

Kara Newman (NoLow Spirits Reviewer)

“I’ve reviewed spirits for Wine Enthusiast for 15 years, running the gamut from lower-proof (vermouths, aperitivo spirits) to new “mid-proof” options (think: vodkas and gins intentionally bottled at half the usual strength) to high-octane whiskies gleefully dubbed as “hazmat.” So it’s been exciting to watch the zero-proof category unfold, and I’ve enjoyed adding a few choice bottles to my at-home bar. I’m looking forward to broadening my experience with N/A spirits as I add the category to my reviewing role.”

Kara’s Picks

The Pathfinder

So far, I’ve found that the aperitivo space is where N/A spirits really shine. Distilled from hemp and layered with botanicals like saffron, ginger, and Douglas fir, this is sort of amaro-esque but isn’t trying to mimic anything in particular.

$40 The Pathfinder

Novara by Bark & Bitter

Founded by veteran bartender Nick Nemeth, no surprise this is particularly mixable. It’s a Campari-ish bittersweet sipper, ideal for building non-alc Negronis or Americanos.

$38 Bark & Bitter

Lyre’s Italian Spritz

More sweet-bitter than bittersweet, this is the move for a zero-proof Spritz. Don’t skimp on the garnishes (orange wheel and olives, please!)

$38 Lyre’s

Abe Zarate (NoLow Wine Reviewer)

“I quit drinking in 2020, joining the demographic looking for more inclusive, high-quality beverage options. As a sober sommelier, I still deal with traditional wine, but that has expanded into creating spaces where two perceived opposites coexist and thrive. I dove into dealcoholized wines early, looking for the best representations. Over the years, I’ve found brands that became favorites, not because they’re all the best, but because I’ve experienced their evolution. And that evolution keeps tasting better and better.”

Abe’s Picks

Oddbird Sparkling Orange

This Alsatian-style, skin-contact sparkler has a surprisingly restrained personality, yet one that is sneakily memorable.

$50 The Zero Proof

Noughty Sparkling Rosé

This is the first dealcoholized wine I tasted that felt like it could fool me.

$23 The Zero Proof

Oceano Zero Chardonnay

A vinous, single-vineyard, single-vintage expression of Chardonnay that showcases all the best parts of wine.

$45 Oceano

Cheron Cowan (NoLow RTD Reviewer)

“It is my great pleasure to begin reviewing NA and low-alcohol RTD beverages. As a 30-year hospitality industry veteran, I have personally had to address my relationship with alcohol and confront over-indulgence. As such, in recent years I have adopted a more holistic approach to my drinking schedule and have introduced more balanced practices to when and how much I imbibe. I take great joy in finding new products that will facilitate drinking with enjoyment, but celebrate other stimulating ingredients than alcohol.”

Cheron’s Picks

Good Twin NA Sparkling White Wine

This zero-proof wine is my favorite as it is very, very low sugar. There is an herbal refreshing component, as well. But the low sugar and effervescence make it a food-friendly pairing wine.

$23 Good Twin

Society de la Rassi Sparkling Rose Beso Besa

This, too, is low sugar. But the mousse is very fine. There is a floralness, too that is very inviting. It is lean textured, but vibrant in terms of its acidity. Again, it’s a great food-pairing counterpart.

$50 Boisson

St. Agrestis Phony Negroni

Great herbalness to this product. It keeps many of the botanicals one would expect in a negroni: wormwood, gentian root, coriander, juniper…It is truly like sipping on a cocktail without the booze. 

$6 St. Agrestis

We invite you to follow along as we begin our journey through this exciting and growing category. If you would like to submit your NoLow wines, spirits, or RTDs for consideration please see the details here.

title: Wine Enthusiast Launches Dedicated No/Low Alcohol Tasting Program To Elevate Growing Beverage Category
summary:
The industry leader is expanding reviews with new 5-star rating system built for non-alcoholic and low-abv wines, spirits, and RTD beverages.

The post Wine Enthusiast Launches Dedicated No/Low Alcohol Tasting Program To Elevate Growing Beverage Category appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
VALHALLA, N.Y. (October 2, 2026) — Wine Enthusiast Companies, a leading global authority on wine, spirits, and beverage culture, announced the launch of its new NoLow rating system and blind-tasting program today. Designed to evaluate no- and low-alcohol wines, spirits, and ready-to-drink (RTD) beverages, the program provides consumers with a reliable guide for discovery while establishing a formal feedback loop for an evolving category.

As consumer preferences expand, there has been a surge in demand for high-quality non-alcoholic and low-abv beverages. In the US alone, non-alcoholic retail sales crossed $1 billion by the end of 2025. Wine Enthusiast’s new NoLow program reflects the brand’s commitment to adapting alongside the beverage industry and supporting producers who are driving innovation in the space. 

“No- and low-alcohol beverages are not just a passing trend. Nielsen reports that 92% of consumers who buy non-alcoholic products also buy alcohol, meaning this is largely the same consumer already looking to our scores for guidance,” said Jacqueline Strum, Editor & Publisher of Wine Enthusiast Media. “Our new NoLow blind-tasting program gives this growing category the attention it deserves, spotlighting quality products and helping consumers make confident choices.”

All NoLow products will adhere to Wine Enthusiast’s rigorous, independent blind-tasting protocol to ensure ratings integrity. Wine Enthusiast’s traditional tasting program uses a 100-point scale that accounts for a product’s ageability, alcohol balance, and other aspects associated with traditionally fermented alcoholic beverages. However, NoLow beverages are produced using distinct methods—such as dealcoholization or custom blending—and are crafted for immediate consumption. Therefore, they cannot be compared 1:1 with classically fermented or distilled beverages. To properly evaluate these products on their own merits, Wine Enthusiast is introducing a tailored 5-Star Rating System:

Outstanding; category-defining.

Exceptional and original.

Well-crafted and highly recommended.

Enjoyable and approachable.

Dependable choice for broad appeal.

Reviews will consider factors including balance, flavor, aroma, texture, and overall drinking experience, with products evaluated within the context of their respective category. In addition to being reviewed, select products will also be included in new annual NoLow Top Lists that highlight stand-out beverages. 

“A five-star rating should mean something. We gathered input from the trade, our tasting team, and the program’s reviewers to define quality across the NoLow category and develop the star rating system. The result is a rating consumers can understand, trust, and use,” said Anna-Christina Cabrales, Tasting Director of Wine Enthusiast.

Wine Enthusiast’s NoLow Tasting Program is spearheaded by seasoned industry experts Abe Zarate, Kara Newman, and Cheron Cowan.

Abe Zarate (NoLow Wine): Abe is Wine Director at New York City’s Crane Club and has led wine programs at Corkbuzz, Intersect by Lexus, and Contento. In 2024, he was named one of Wine Enthusiast’s Future 40 Tastemakers. Known as SoberSomm on Instagram, Abe is an advocate for conscious consumption and building a more inclusive wine industry. 

Kara Newman (NoLow Spirits): Kara is a writer-at-large and veteran spirits reviewer for Wine Enthusiast. An accomplished journalist whose work has appeared in The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and Food & Wine, she is also the author of seven popular cocktail books, including Shake.Stir.Sip. and Nightcap.

Cheron Cowan (NoLow RTDs & Others): Cheron is an Advanced Sommelier with the Court of Master Sommeliers and reviews American wines from the Midwest and the East Coast for Wine Enthusiast. She brings years of high-profile restaurant leadership experience (including Esca, Blue Hill NYC, and Gramercy Tavern) and international recognition as the inaugural winner of the Becky Wasserman Burgundy Scholarship.

Samples can be submitted via the Wine Enthusiast Ratings Platform (WERP) for a fee of $95 per SKU, which guarantees a blind-tasted star rating and written review. Low-alcohol products between 0.5% and 10% abv are eligible for the NoLow program when they are produced and marketed specifically as low-alcohol alternatives. Traditional alcoholic beverages that naturally fall within this abv should continue to be evaluated through Wine Enthusiast’s existing 100-point scale.

For details on submission guidelines or to view upcoming ratings, visit www.wineenthusiast.com or contact submissionssupport@wineenthusiast.com.

The post Wine Enthusiast Ratings Platform: Frequently Asked Questions appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Wine Enthusiast Ratings Platform: FAQs

Table of Contents

  • Before You Submit
  • After You Submit
  • Processing Fee
  • Shipping and Customs
  • Status Updates and Review Timing
  • Reviewers & Regions
  • Shipping Information & Addresses

Shipping Information by Geographic Region

  • Eastern USA & Most of World
  • USA: California Central Coast & Southern California
  • USA: Northern CA & California AVA, AR, CO, IL, KS, MO, NE, NV, OK, UT
  • USA: Napa County & Sonoma County CA, AZ, LA, NM, TX
  • USA: OR, WA, AK, HI, ID, IA, MN, MT, ND, SD, WI, WY, CANADA
  • France: Bordeaux, Southwest France & Corsica
  • Spain (John Sumners regions) & Portugal

Shipping Information by Product

  • Spirits & RTDs
  • Non Alcoholic and Low Alcoholic products

Before You Submit

What products can I submit for review?

Wine Enthusiast will review:

  • Wines (100% grape-based only)
  • Spirits
  • Ready-to-Drink (RTD) products
  • Non-alcoholic and low-alcohol versions of all the above

Samples submitted must be finished and properly labeled. Unfinished and/or unlabeled samples are not accepted. All product samples must be entered into the Wine Enthusiast Ratings Platform to receive a review.

Does my product have to be imported in order to receive a review?

All products meeting the above criteria are welcome to be reviewed and rated, including products not yet imported to the U.S. 

Please note, Wine Enthusiast does not provide customs and import documentation. For assistance with customs & import logistics, European producers may wish to engage our partner service, 3P Wine. We look forward to expanding this service to other regions in the near future.

Why are non-alcoholic and low alcoholic (No-Low) products rated differently?

Wine Enthusiast provides two rating scales depending on the style of the product reviewed. 

Wines and spirits receive a numerical point score out of 100. These ratings take into account the immediate character of the product as well as its aging potential. 

Ready-to-Drink products and all low-alcohol branded and non-alcoholic beverages intended for immediate consumption are rated on a five-star scale. No-Low products are produced differently. They have a different structural profile from traditional wine and spirits, and are not intended for long-term cellaring. 

Dealcoholization and alternative production methods affect the nature of No-Low products, so these cannot be scored alongside wines that undergo vastly different techniques. 

The star rating reflects quality at release and point of consumption.

What counts as non-alcoholic or low alcohol?

Non-alcoholic products must have an alcohol by volume (abv) below 0.5%.

Submissions may be marked as low-alcohol if they have an abv between 0.5% to 10%. Note, the ‘low-alcohol’ category is intended for products that intentionally feature a lower abv or equivalent branding on their front label, for example “only 8%” or “light”. These are partially de-alcoholized after fermentation. 

Traditionally-made wines with lower alcohol should elect to be rated and reviewed under Wine Enthusiast’s 100-point scoring system. Examples of these include dessert style and sweet wines (e.g. Moscato d’Asti, Sauternes, etc). These lower-alcohol wines are the product of traditional winemaking, and the 100-point scale considers their potential to develop with age.

After You Submit

Where do I send my samples?

Please see the full section Shipping & Customs below.

When will I receive my review?

While we guarantee your sample will be reviewed, we cannot guarantee that reviews will be completed within a specific timeframe. Once they’re checked in, wines are rested in our cellar to protect against bottle shock. To ensure balanced tasting flights, it may be necessary to wait until we receive similar vintages, regions, varietals etc. to the product you have submitted. So while this means the timeline from submission to published review can vary, we adhere to these protocols to ensure your product receives a fair review.

Where will my wine/spirit review appear?

All qualifying reviews are published online at wineenthusiast.com/ratings. Select reviews will appear in the print magazine. All wine reviews posted to the Wine Enthusiast website are considered final. Once a review is posted, it cannot be edited or deleted. By submitting your product for review, you grant Wine Enthusiast the right to publish it, in whole or in part, on our website and to any of our editorial needs and discretion. Reviews are separate from editorial coverage.

Are there deadlines to submit products for review?

Currently, Wine Enthusiast accepts wines and ready-to-drink beverages on a rolling basis; you can submit your sample as soon as your wine or RTD is packaged and labeled for sale. Unfinished and tank samples are not accepted. Spirit producers can refer to the 2027 Spirits Review Calendar to determine when to submit.

What does my score mean?

100-POINT RATING SCALE

STAR RATING SCALE

Outstanding; category-defining.

Exceptional and original.

Well-crafted and highly recommended.

Enjoyable and approachable.

Dependable choice for broad appeal.

How can I view and share my review?

All qualifying wine and spirit reviews are published online at wineenthusiast.com/ratings.

Select reviews will appear in the print magazine in addition to reviews with a purchased print label. All wine reviews posted to the Wine Enthusiast website are considered final. Once a review is posted, it cannot be edited or deleted. By submitting your product for review, you grant Wine Enthusiast the right to publish it, in whole or in part, on our website and to any of our editorial needs and discretion. Reviews are separate from editorial coverage.

Processing Fee

What does the processing fee cover?

There is a processing fee of $95 per SKU. This processing fee supports the Wine Enthusiast Ratings Platform operations; the administrative, staffing, and logistical needs to maintain the ethical blind-tasting standard; and the production of the buying guides. The processing fee does not speed up the publication of your review and has no bearing on your final score. Reviewers will continue to taste without knowledge of whose product is in front of them.

Shipping & Customs

Where do I ship my samples?

Shipping locations vary according to the country and region of origin, as well as the type of product you have submitted. Please refer to the Reviewers & Regions assignment list and the respective shipping addresses detailed below.

What samples do I need to send?

Wines: Please include two bottles for each submission.

RTDs: Please include two bottles/cans/boxes for each submission.

Spirits: Please send one bottle per submission.

All samples must be finished products and labeled ready for sale. Unfinished samples are not accepted.

What do I have to include with my shipment?

Once you have completed your Ratings Platform submission, print out the Shipment Barcode (QR code) sheet. Include this sheet inside each box with your samples. Please pack your products in recyclable materials. Submissions sent in packages made from Styrofoam delay our processing time.

How are shipping fees and customs fees handled?

Shipping fees, custom fees, and duty fees are the full responsibility of the submitter. The submitter is responsible for coordinating logistics and covering all costs related to the delivery of wine/spirit sample submissions to the correct review location.

Can you assist with customs and import documentation?

The submitter is responsible for managing customs documentation and meeting U.S. legal requirements, including but not limited to:

  • COLA (Certificate of Label Approval) Waiver(s)
  • FDA Prior Notice filing
  • Importer Permits and tax identification
  • Customs Taxes, Duties, and Registration
  • Power of Attorney
  • Certificate of Age and Origin Requirements

If your product is imported, Wine Enthusiast recommends samples be shipped by the brand’s U.S. importer. 

Our import clearing partner can provide customs and logistics assistance to brands not yet imported to the U.S. 

Submitters looking to use this service should consult 3P Wine prior to making their submission in the Wine Enthusiast Ratings Platform. Please note, this service is currently only available for European-based producers.

Status Updates & Review Timing

Have you received my samples?

Wine Enthusiast blind tastes and rates approximately 25,000 wines and spirits every year. Please retain your tracking information and check with your carrier on the status of your shipment’s delivery. Please be aware that within the Wine Enthusiast Ratings Platform, the date your sample(s) changes status to “Checked In” is not always the same as the date of delivery.

How do I find out when my wine/spirit has been reviewed and scored?

You may log in to the Ratings Platform at any time to check for status updates of your product submission.

When your wine is selected for publication in an upcoming issue, the Wine Enthusiast sales team will contact you via email to share your embargoed score.

What each Ratings Platform status means:

Submitted: You have successfully entered your product on the Wine Enthusiast Ratings Platform. You are ready to ship your samples along with the Shipment Barcodes (QR Code) sheet to the reviewer for your product or region. If you need to change any of the details submitted, you may also request an edit.

Pending Check In: If you have requested an edit to your submission information, this status will display until the sample(s) are received and the edit can be verified by a member of our Tasting Department.

Pending Edit: When you see this status, Wine Enthusiast staff are requesting you to verify a change to your submitted information. We may also email you directly if we need to confirm a difference between the sample we receive and the submitted information.

Checked In: This status indicates that a member of the Wine Enthusiast Tasting Department has unpacked your submission and confirmed the samples received match the submitted information. This also confirms your sample meets all eligibility requirements. 

Please note: the Check In date is not always the same as the date of delivery. To check if your shipment has arrived at its review location, please contact your carrier for proof of delivery.

Reviewed: This status lets you know your wine has been flighted and tasted by your region’s expert reviewer. Your product is progressing in the publication process, but the score is not yet visible to you. Reviews must first be prepared for publication before the scores are shared. 

Ready for Purchase: When you see this status, your wine has been rated and assigned to an upcoming magazine issue. The review is not yet public. A member of the Wine Enthusiast Sales team will contact you via email with options for purchasing a label package within the Buying Guide. This includes the option to purchase an express review, and obtain an official WE Rating Logo allowing you to promote your score earlier. If you see this status and have not received an email, please contact labelsales@wineenthusiast.com and include the product’s WERP ID in your subject line.

Published: The score and review of your product is posted on wineenthusiast.com/ratings. You can now share your score and use your review in marketing materials.

content:
Your Fall Wine Lineup: Crisp Whites and a Crowd-Pleasing Red

The early days of autumn live somewhere between summer and fall, demanding wines that complement the best the season has to offer. In many parts of the country, warm, sun-drenched days are met with a welcome whisper of cool air, suggesting tablescapes of heartier fare and food-friendly wines are within imminent reach. With Wente Family Vineyards, celebrating autumn’s arrival is as easy as popping the cork on one of the estate’s ecologically-conscious wines, featuring grape varieties and styles that promise to shine alongside the season’s most cherished flavors.

Great bottles needn’t require a special occasion; in fact, the right bottle can become a celebratory moment itself. When produced from high-quality fruit and thoughtful farming, everyday wines easily turn the ordinary into extraordinary, making accessible bottles feel effortlessly premium. How do you find “the one”? Stick with exceptional producers that focus on place, people, and the preservation of resources. For over 140 years, Wente Family Vineyards has pioneered America’s viticultural legacy. Regarded as one of the country’s oldest continuously owned and operated wineries, the estate is now overseen by the family’s fifth generation, who continues to craft versatile, thoughtfully produced bottles from certified sustainable vineyards, proving that quality and value can exist within the same bottle.

When warm afternoons and cool evenings meet, versatility and food-friendliness are the key to selecting a bottle. For days that begin beneath the early fall sun, Wente’s Pacific Mist Pinot Grigio (a 90-point Best Buy from Wine Enthusiast) is well-suited to meet the moment. Crisp and refreshing, it’s an ideal accompaniment to late-season picnics, post-work appetizers, and easy weeknight meals alike, with flavors of green apple, pear, and refreshing white peach. Similarly, Wente’s Louis Mel Sauvignon Blanc (another Wine Enthusiast Best Buy) comes to life on warm afternoons. Vibrant and energetic, notes of grapefruit, citrus, and tropical fruit come to life alongside seasonal salads, fresh herbs, and farmers’ market-inspired dishes, backed by palate-cleansing acidity and a long, persistent finish.

As the evening chill settles in, Wente Family Vineyards Morning Fog Chardonnay (Best Buy, Wine Enthusiast) brings comfort. Richer in style, the wine beautifully bridges the gap between daytime sun and end-of-day freshness, pairing perfectly with roasted chicken, creamy pastas, and early fall produce. Beloved for its balance of bright fruit and restrained oak influence, it offers exceptional value while promising to appeal to a wide variety of white wine drinkers. For cooler fall evenings and game-day entertaining, Wente Baily Hill Pinot Noir fits the bill. These light-bodied and invigorating bottles boast fruit-forward flavors of cherry, wild strawberry, and raspberry. It shows its best sipped alongside pizza, mushroom-based recipes, and all things grilled, especially when enjoyed with a slight chill.

While the arrival of autumn tends to mark the return of structured routines, one of the easiest ways to ease back into busy schedules is to prioritize carving out time to connect with friends and loved ones. As school calendars and sports agendas pick back up, Wente Family Vineyards diverse portfolio of wines meet wine drinkers where they’re at, adding a refreshing dimension to tailgates, backyard dinner parties, and casual weeknight gatherings alike.

Each bottle from Wente Family Vineyards showcases a historic moment in America’s winemaking legacy, while also appealing to fans of varietal-specific wines of all styles. The wide-ranging bottle lineup fully embodies the Wente family philosophy: great wine should be versatile, delicious, and accessible at any price point, as well as worthy of sharing around a full table during any moment of the year. 

Above all, great bottles of wine remain one of the easiest ways to elevate everyday moments. From harvest-inspired dinners al fresco to casual weeknight meals at home, popping the cork on a Wente Family Vineyards’ wine ensures seasonal complement and food pairing versatility, with industry-approved quality and generations-old expertise at the core of each bottle. 

To learn more about Wente Family Vineyards, visit https://wentevineyards.com/journal/.

title: Why Agave Spirits Deserve the Same Consideration as Wine
summary:
The point isn’t to force tequila and mezcal into a wine-shaped box, but to bring the same curiosity and attention to both.

The post Why Agave Spirits Deserve the Same Consideration as Wine appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
At an agave spirits tasting at Muna Restaurant at Nobu Hotel Los Cabos, I expected tequila and mezcal. Instead, one glass after another arrived bearing drinks with names I barely knew—and flavors I hadn’t known agave could contain.

There were spirits that tasted saline and windswept, others floral and tropical. I found wet stone, roasted pineapple, green herbs, a yogurt-like tang, damp earth, and the savory funk of a cheese rind. The smoke I knew to expect with agave-based liquors was sometimes present, but it was only one note in a much larger composition. I was blown away by the nuance, depth, and sheer deliciousness of it all—the multitudes agave could contain and express. The tasting experience reminded me of learning to love wine: the realization that what’s in your glass is a record of a plant, a place, the weather, fermentation, and the hand of the maker.

Wine vocabulary can offer a useful doorway into understanding agave spirits. The point isn’t to force tequila and mezcal into a wine-shaped box, but to bring the same curiosity and attention to both.

Begin with ‘Small Kisses’

According to Ana María Martínez Núñez, director of food and beverage at Nobu Hotel Los Cabos, tequila and mezcal should be enjoyed in, as she puts it, “small kisses. They’re not meant to be taken as shots. They’re meant to be savored slowly.” 

Pour a small amount into a glass that gives the aromas room to gather. Then wait. Sergio Mendoza, co-founder of Tequila Don Fulano, recommends allowing tequila to breathe for a few minutes so the ethanol begins to lift and the aroma of cooked agave can emerge. Unlike wine, it doesn’t need vigorous swirling; a gentle movement of the glass is plenty to bring out the bouquet.

Rather than plunging your nose into the glass, approach it gradually. Martínez Núñez takes several short passes. The first may smell mostly of alcohol, but on the second or third, flowers, citrus, herbs, fruit, spices, minerals, and cooked agave begin to come forward.

Then take a tiny sip. Let it move slowly across your tongue. This is not a test, and there is no prize for identifying the “correct” fruit. You’re simply noticing what the spirit brings to mind.

Taste Texture, Not Just Flavor

Wine drinkers are used to considering acidity, tannin, and body. Agave spirits have their own structural vocabulary. Does the spirit feel silky, creamy, or oily? Is it crisp and cleansing, or dry and gently gripping? Mendoza explains that residual oils, agave fibers, and distillation choices can influence the weight and texture of a liquor.

Notice how the flavors evolve. Citrus, flowers, or ripe fruit may give way to herbs, pepper, earthiness, or savoriness. Then consider the finish: Does the flavor disappear, or keep unfolding after you swallow? And resist relying too heavily on “smooth.” A spirit can be easy to drink and still be bland. Heat, pepper, minerality, or savory complexity are not necessarily flaws.

“What truly matters is balance, the integration of alcohol and the spirit’s ability to express where it came from,” says Martínez Núñez.

Follow the Plant, Place, and Producer

Thinking of agave species like grape varieties can help orient wine drinkers: Espadín may show citrus, fresh herbs, and cooked agave. Tobalá can be floral and aromatic, while Tepeztate may offer herbs, minerals, and white pepper. Cuishe can lean vegetal and mineral, sometimes with lactic notes reminiscent of yogurt or kefir.

But plant variety is only the beginning. Soil, elevation, climate, and biodiversity all affect the plant—and agave may take anywhere from 6 to more than 30 years to mature. A wine grape reflects one growing season; an agave embodies years or decades of weather and agricultural decisions.

Agaves from the Highlands of Jalisco are often associated with floral, fruity expressions, while those from the Tequila Valley may emphasize herbs, black pepper, minerality, olives, or earth.

“I like to think of it like painting,” says Leon Bañuelos Jr., a third-generation tequilero with Tequila El Mexicano. “Highland agave gives the maestro tequilero a broader palette to work with—more sugar, more nuance, more dimension.” Bañuelos also cautions against thinking of agave as simply sweet. “Agave is more than just a sweet smell,” he says. “It can also be very herbaceous and have notes of citrus.”

Then comes the maker. Cooking, fermentation, water, still type, and proof all leave sensory fingerprints. Slow cooking can develop roasted sweetness; long fermentation may build aromatic complexity; distillation choices can shape texture and savoriness. As Martínez Núñez puts it, “The agave writes the story, and the producer decides how to tell it.”

Read the Label Like a Curious Drinker

A label won’t tell you everything, but it can give you a place to begin. For tequila, look for “100% agave,” rather than a mixto made with additional sugars. Find the four-digit NOM number, which identifies the licensed distillery where the tequila was produced. Looking into that number can reveal which other brands come from the same facility and offer a clearer sense of who is behind the bottle.

For tequila, mezcal, and other agave spirits, look for the agave species, the region in which it was grown, or where and who made it—the producer, the master distiller, the communities. Details about cooking, fermentation, still type, maturation, and sourcing also offer avenues of exploration into the story each spirit tells.

At a bar or bottle shop, ask simple questions: Who made this? Where was the agave grown? How mature was it? Was it cooked slowly or processed more quickly? Was fermentation spontaneous, or were accelerants used? What does the producer do particularly well?

It doesn’t have to be an interrogation, just a conversation. One of Martínez Núñez’s favorite questions is also the most inviting: “What’s the story behind this bottle?”

Don’t Confuse Rarity with Quality

Words such as “wild,” “rare,” and “limited edition” can make an agave spirit sound irresistible. But scarcity alone says nothing about flavor, craftsmanship or responsibility.

Some agaves take decades to mature, and rising demand can put enormous pressure on plants, landscapes, and communities. Before becoming dazzled by rarity, ask how the agave was harvested and whether the producer is working to ensure that it will still exist 20 or 30 years from now.

Responsible production can include replanting, protecting biodiversity, managing water and firewood carefully, reusing by-products, and fairly supporting the families and communities that have preserved these traditions.

“Exclusivity creates desire,” Martínez Núñez says. “But sustainability creates legacy.” 

Most of all, allow yourself to taste without rushing to rank. A saline note may remind one person of oysters and another of sea air. An herbal aroma might evoke rosemary, tomato leaf, cactus, or a family garden. Your sensory memories belong in the glass, too.

Wine can teach us how much pleasure comes from paying attention. Agave spirits ask us to pay attention differently: one landscape, one story, and one small kiss at a time.

  2. Shake up some 'varietal vodka' into your next martini.
  3. Bourbon lotteries allow consumers access to rare bottles at a good price, but the competition is heating up.
  4. Forget house wines. Restaurants are making their own house spirits too.
  5. Newly available in the U.S., still-strength tequila is taking over.

title: Halloween Bars Are Scary Profitable
summary:
Halloween is one of the strongest sales drivers for bars and restaurants. Why not make it last longer?

The post Halloween Bars Are Scary Profitable appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Key Points

  • Pop-up franchises like Black Lagoon help bars extend single-night Halloween crowds into a lucrative, month-long revenue stream.
  • Immersive seasonal menus allow high-end cocktail lounges to attract group traffic and capitalize on holiday spending.
  • Driven by a growing demand for escapism, year-round spooky bars and extended events succeed long after October ends.

For many bargoers, visiting one of the myriad Christmas-themed pop-ups that roll out in December has become an annual rite. Bars count on the business that these programs bring in, too.

Increasingly, hospitality pros are hoping to replicate that magic—and profitability—with Halloween-themed pop-ups that extend beyond spooky season.

For the past six years, a “goth-tropical” franchise called Black Lagoon has been the front-runner in the Halloween bar biz, transforming bars across North America with eerie, cinematic décor and themed drinks like the Moon Shadow (nutmeg-infused vodka, banana liqueur, and cold brew coffee). In 2026, 34 venues are slated to participate.

Co-founded by Erin Hayes and Kelsey Ramage, both based in Los Angeles, Black Lagoon began as a post-pandemic pop-up. 

“We love the witchy vibes, the celebratory aspects of it,” Hayes says. “Kelsey had found a place to rent for the month of October, and it was successful beyond what we had imagined. We had people lined up around the block every night. People loved the weird and wonderful vibe that we were putting out.”

Over time, their pop-up grew into a franchise. Bars pay a fee to rebrand as a Black Lagoon for the month. In turn, they receive creepy tropical mugs and other glassware; a six-drink menu that spotlights a handful of brand sponsors, including Teremana tequila, Kraken rum, and Mr. Black cold brew coffee liqueur; a lookbook for décor; and playlists.

“We try to make it plug-and-play,” Hayes says. “We say, ‘Here are the things you need for your success, now it’s up to you to put it into play.’ They can do whatever they want to dress up the space, we just ask them to keep to the menu.”

Black Lagoon’s success hasn’t gone unnoticed. This year, New York City-based Cocktail Kingdom Hospitality Group, the team behind super popular Christmas-themed pop-ups Miracle and Sippin’ Santa, is getting into the mix with The Haunting, a similar franchise of Halloween-themed immersive pop-up bars.

The mood skews more nostalgic than goth, leaning into childhood haunted houses for aesthetic inspiration and trick-or-treat bags for drinks like the Scream-sicle (tequila, spiced vanilla liqueur, carrot and orange cordial, and habanero). 

About 40 bars—most of which are already part of the Miracle franchise—are slated to participate in the month-long pop-up. There are locations across the United States and in London and Oslo. The business model is similar to Miracle and Black Lagoon: bars pay a fee to participate, and receive recipes and physical menus (unlike Black Lagoon, brand sponsors are not designated), social media assets, and branded merch. The latter includes mugs resembling colorful cauldrons or creepy doll heads, created by Cocktail Kingdom and available for purchase.

Treats for Some Bars, Tricks for Others

Halloween presents an oddly uneven playing ground for bars.

For traditional bars and taverns, it’s a bonanza: The Saturday before or after Halloween consistently ranks among the top ten days of the year for drinking venues in the U.S., according to Nielsen’s NIQ BeverageTrak. 

In 2025, it was the eighth busiest night of the year, as measured by sales value at the average outlet. It ranked behind St. Patrick’s Day in the number-one spot, as well as sports events like the official kickoff of the MLB Division Series, March Madness, and the NFL regular season opening week.

“Halloween is one of the strongest sales drivers for bars and restaurants because it turns a night out into a full-fledged occasion,” says Matt Crompton, vice president of On Premise for NIQ. 

The occasion gives people a specific reason to go out, particularly in groups, so bars see higher-than-normal amounts of weekend traffic. Consumers are willing to spend more on themed cocktails and other premium drinks, too. 

“Combined with broad appeal across age groups and the amplifying power of social media, Halloween consistently ranks among the top revenue-generating days of the year for drinking venues,” Crompton says.

However, intimate bars that focus on high-end drinks typically don’t see the same results, says Greg Boehm, founder and CEO of Cocktail Kingdom Hospitality Group. “Halloween is a bad night for cocktail bars.” 

The Miracle team is hoping a monthlong spooky season pop-up might help turn that around. 

“It’s about extending the season and having a good time,” Boehm says. “It’s not about having a Halloween day—it’s about having a Halloween season, like we did with Miracle.”

Halloween Every Day?

Of course, many bars trick out for Halloween independent of either franchise. And a committed handful celebrate the macabre all year round, such as NYC’s Paradise Lost, Los Angeles’s Beetle House, and spots like Vampire Café or The Crypt in New Orleans, a city that proudly boasts dozens of haunted and/or gothic bars, regardless of the season. 

But perhaps the longest-running year-round stalwart is Jekyl and Hyde, a Pittsburgh bar marking its 30th anniversary in 2026. (Its Instagram tagline reads, “Celebrating Halloween every day.”)

The space started as a typical neighborhood spot near East Carson Street, a main drag in the South Side neighborhood noted for its high concentration of bars, recalls owner Mike Alberter. When a regular customer who was in the business of building haunted houses offered to donate ghostly trappings after the season wrapped, Alberter saw an opportunity to make his bar stand out. Year after year, he added more black lights, fake cobwebs, miniature skulls, and more.

“There’s stuff on the ceilings, the walls,” Alberter says. “We put little spider rings into the drinks. We have candy out every day, like trick or treat.” 

While the two weeks leading up to Halloween are always packed, he says, business is steady all year long. Events like horror film screenings and “scary-oke” karaoke nights bring in costumed revelers eager to sip drinks including the signature Jac-O-Lantern (vanilla vodka, orange cream liqueur, orange juice, Sprite, and whipped cream).

“People love Halloween all year long [because] they love to dress up and be whoever,” he says. “I feel like Halloween is bigger than Christmas, in terms of money spent.”

Experiences and Escapism

Black Lagoon’s proprietors have opted to inject extra ghoulish glee into immersive events spanning beyond October. Hayes and Ramage also run Krampus Cove around the holidays, and recently expanded into the warmer months with their Summerween-inspired Bad Witch goth-girl pool parties. 

“People are looking for experiences more than anything,” Ramage observes. “Things are tough and heavy in terms of the world right now. The dollar is stretched. People want to go out and do more than just have drinks. People want to escape the world and enjoy some silly spookiness.”

Adding to that endeavor, mass merchandisers have steadily stretched the Halloween sales season earlier and earlier, erasing the gap between Summerween and All Hallow’s Eve. 

“We see Disney and Universal and the home décor stores are dropping their décor August 1,” Ramage says. That’s not necessarily a bad thing, either. “Halloween isn’t just October 31,” she says. “You can have Halloween vibes anytime.”

title: The World’s Largest Wine Cellar Is a 124-Mile-Long Treasure Trove
summary:
Far from a traditional wine cellar, the storage complex at Mileștii Mici in Moldova feels like an underground city.

The post The World’s Largest Wine Cellar Is a 124-Mile-Long Treasure Trove appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
It is a warm June day in Moldova when I arrive at Mileștii Mici, home to the largest cellar complex in the world. Situated among lush green landscapes in a town of the same name, the winery is a roughly 45-minute drive from the capital Chisinau and an hour and a half from the border with Ukraine. 

Its collection made the Guinness Book of World Records in 2007, when the cellars held about 1.5 million bottles; the stock count lasted several months. Even at Mileștii Mici, no one knows the exact current number, but estimates go up to 2 million. (I imagine a stock count now could take a year.)

A small electric train transports me through dark, subterranean surroundings until I am about 260 feet below ground—that’s at least 20 stories into the earth. It’s chilly down here, so I put on a jacket as I study the bottles around me. In the dim light, the oldest one I spot is from 1969. But soon it dawns on me that a great chunk of them come from one particular year: 1986.

Pedro, my guide, explains that it’s because of Mikhail Gorbachev. The last leader of the Soviet Union was convinced that his people drank too much, and so in 1986 he introduced strict rules that limited the purchase and sale of alcohol. Gorbachev’s “dry law” introduced quotas and rationing that led to overproduction relative to consumption. This era lasted around four years, Pedro says, and Soviets were limited to buying a few bottles per month per person. 

During this time, authorities destroyed wine supplies throughout the Soviet Union, of which Moldova was still a part. Fearful for their own stores, the owners of Mileștii Mici (founded in 1969, go figure) built secret rooms underground to protect their most rare and expensive bottles. There’s an irony there somewhere that Gorbachev could not have predicted: His prohibition led to an abundance of wine, a treasure trove of 1.5 million bottles or more, that has outlasted even him.

A Charming Hodgepodge of Wine and History

To say that the wine cellar at Mileștii Mici is enormous would be an understatement. The total length of the galleries is 200 kilometers (about 124 miles), of which about 55 kilometers (about 34 miles) are currently in use. The place was originally a limestone mine, in operation since 1886, and converted into a wine cellar in the late 1960s. Aesthetically, it’s all a bit of a charming hodgepodge: some sections have designs that gesture to old feudal castles, others to ancient Greek temples. 

Far from a traditional wine cellar, the storage complex at Mileștii Mici feels like an underground city, one through which you can actually drive your car. The scale of the place is massive, as are the thousands of oak barrels. Made in the 1970s and ’80s using wood imported from what is now Ukraine and Russia, the barrels have capacities that range from 600 to 2,000 wine decaliters.

Moldova’s wine culture is deeply rooted in the country’s history and identity, yet many international visitors know very little about it. One cannot find a better introduction to Moldovan wines than a visit to the Mileștii Mici wine cellar—or rather, city. 

At the end of the tour, guests can enjoy a glass or two of Moldovan wines accompanied with nibbles served in elegant tasting halls. On my visit, I indulge in a delicious plate of prosciutto crudo, salami, carpaccio, breadsticks, mixed nuts, and figs served with a young 2024 Chardonnay and a 2021 Cabernet Sauvignon. Sometimes, I’m told, these tastings even have live music played by Moldovan musicians.

Mileștii Mici has found creative ways to make use of all that space in the cellars, one of which is a regular race. 

First introduced in 2019, the Mileștii Mici Wineruns has participants running a total length of 10 kilometers (6 miles), part of it in the legendary galleries. According to Anton Zaharov, one of about 500 runners at a recent event, the dashing through those wine-filled stores is novel and unusual, but gets old real quick. 

“Most of the time you’re running through a dark, dimly lit tunnel of dust and sand,” he says. “Only the last two kilometers take you through the winery’s beautiful grounds.” One wine enthusiast’s paradise is one marathoner’s purgatory, it seems. At least they stay cool down there.
